planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into gravelly, sharply drained limestone or igneous rubble; give a season of occasional deep watering to establish the root crown before going fully dry.

directions: Foothill beargrass forms a dense, grass-like rosette of narrow, wiry leaves on rocky slopes and grassland benches across the Trans-Pecos, southern New Mexico, and the sky-island foothills into Chihuahua, usually smaller and more compact than the related Texas bear grass. Tall branched stalks of small cream flowers rise above the foliage in late spring to summer, followed by papery seed capsules that persist into fall. It needs sharply drained, mineral soil and essentially no supplemental water once its root crown is established, making it a tough accent for rock gardens and dry foothill-themed plantings. Avoid heavy, poorly drained soil or overhead irrigation, which rot the crown.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring on limestone-derived, gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; water to establish the first season, then taper to occasional deep soaks.

directions: Big Bend silverleaf is a smaller, smoother-leaved relative of the common cenizo, restricted to limestone slopes and canyon foothills of the Trans-Pecos and adjacent Coahuila, where it forms a rounded shrub with silvery-gray leaves and purple, funnel-shaped flowers that flush heavily after summer rain. It thrives in lean, rocky, alkaline soil with sharp drainage and resents heavy clay or frequent watering, which encourage root rot. Use it where a compact, silver-foliaged accent is wanted in a foothill or canyon xeriscape bed, and prune lightly after bloom flushes to keep a tidy form rather than shearing into a formal hedge.

planting.note: Set transplants on rocky limestone slopes or berms in full sun with excellent drainage; a light first-season watering regime is enough to establish the taproot.

directions: Rock sage grows on rocky limestone and igneous foothill slopes of the Trans-Pecos and adjacent New Mexico, forming a wiry, gray-green subshrub with felted, textured leaves and spikes of lavender-blue flowers that bloom intermittently from spring through fall after rain. It is well adapted to thin, alkaline soil and intense sun, needing almost no irrigation once its woody base is established, and benefits from an occasional hard cutback to keep new, leafier growth. Pair it with other low sky-island foothill shrubs in a dry rock garden, where its silvery texture and long bloom season provide steady interest for native bees.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, rocky, well-drained soil so winter cold helps break seed dormancy; container plants can also be set out in spring.

directions: Big Bend penstemon is a tall, slender perennial of rocky canyon slopes and desert-grassland foothills of the Chisos and Davis Mountains region, sending up stiff spikes of brilliant red, tubular flowers in spring that are a magnet for hummingbirds. It demands lean, gravelly or rocky soil with sharp drainage and full sun, since richer garden soil and frequent watering shorten its lifespan and invite crown rot. Allow seed to set and scatter to maintain a planting over time, and avoid mulch piled against the woody base. It is an excellent accent among boulders in a foothill or canyon-themed xeriscape bed.

planting.note: Scarify seed before sowing, or set out container stock in spring on rocky, well-drained soil in full sun; once rooted it tolerates long dry spells and reflected heat.

directions: Fragrant mimosa is a thorny, nitrogen-fixing shrub of rocky foothills and draws across the Trans-Pecos, Edwards Plateau, and southern Plains, bearing fine, fern-like leaflets and small pink, globe-shaped, sweetly fragrant flower puffs in spring that draw bees and butterflies. It establishes on lean, rocky or caliche soil with minimal care and tolerates hard pruning if it becomes leggy, resprouting readily from the base. Its tangled, thorny habit makes it useful as a wildlife thicket or barrier planting in a dry foothill garden, and its seed pods provide cover and forage once established.

subcategory: Chihuahuan Desert sky-island foothill native shrub

planting.note: Set out container plants in spring on gravelly, well-drained soil in full sun; water regularly the first season, then reduce to occasional deep soaks.

directions: Silver dalea is a fine-textured, silvery-leaved shrub of rocky canyons and sky-island foothills spanning the Trans-Pecos, southern New Mexico, and Arizona borderlands into Mexico, producing slender spikes of small purple pea-like flowers over an unusually long bloom season from fall into winter. As a nitrogen-fixing legume it performs well in lean, gravelly soil and needs little fertilizer, though it is somewhat more cold-sensitive than many Chihuahuan Desert natives and benefits from a protected foothill microclimate in its coldest hardiness range. Light shearing after a bloom flush keeps it full and encourages repeat flowering, and it pairs well with other silver-foliaged xeric shrubs.

planting.note: Plant container-grown offsets or rosettes in spring into sharply drained limestone gravel or rock crevices in full sun; avoid any standing water at the crown.

directions: Slimfoot agave is a small, slow-growing rosette succulent restricted to limestone outcrops and rocky foothill slopes of the Big Bend region of Texas, forming tight clusters of narrow, slender leaves tipped with a sharp terminal spine. Mature rosettes send up a tall, slender flowering stalk once in their lifetime, after which that rosette dies back while offsets continue the clump. It needs rock-garden drainage and almost no irrigation once established, making it ideal for a crevice garden or container planting among other small Trans-Pecos succulents, and it tolerates winter cold well for its size given its native elevation.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out transplants in spring onto rocky or sandy, well-drained grassland soil in full sun; established plants reseed readily and spread along the ground.

directions: Wright's verbena is a low, spreading perennial of rocky desert grassland and foothill flats across the Trans-Pecos, southern New Mexico, and Arizona, producing flat clusters of small pink-to-purple flowers over a long season from spring through fall, especially after summer rain. It roots as it trails and tolerates heavy foot traffic poorly but spreads readily across lean, well-drained soil, making it a good low groundcover between rocks or along a dry grassland border. Deadheading spent flower clusters encourages repeat bloom, and it needs only occasional supplemental water beyond natural rainfall once established.
sources: Native Plant Society of New Mexico
